source.title: TravelBench : Exploring LLM Performance in Low-Resource Domains

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; the scaling results are primarily conveyed in figures, with no plotted values transcribed in the text.
record.tranche_reason: It tests downstream benchmark performance against approximate training compute, using a different measure and setting from pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an aggregate performance-versus-compute trend and Qwen3-family performance variation across tasks, which bear on V6. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit or test power laws, extrapolate from smaller runs, or compare compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. The reasoning-on/off comparison is not included as a scaling-law result: it measures the effect of enabling reasoning, not the claim's scaling relation. Scaling-law statements in Related Works are citations, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: It reports downstream travel-domain benchmark performance against approximate training compute across open models, and against model size within the Qwen3 family. This bears on V6 in a new, low-resource domain setting. It is not a same-question new method (T2): there is no fitted law and no loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that out-of-the-box LLMs reach performance bottlenecks on domain-specific travel tasks despite more parameters and training tokens, with diminishing non-linear gains in compute, and that performance is strongly task-dependent. They add that reasoning boosts smaller models more than larger ones.
record.recipe_differences: Uses instruct-tuned models and a cross-model comparison of composite downstream benchmark performance against approximate FLOPs; it does not train models, measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, or test extrapolation or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that models may respond differently to prompts, but use one prompt across models; some large models are quantised, and some closed-source model size and training-data details are unavailable.

fits_no_version.finding: Enabling reasoning helps smaller Qwen3 models but gives little or negative gain for larger ones (235B degrades).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of test-time reasoning to downstream performance shrinks with model size.

record.problems: The scaling figures provide no numeric values in the text; the study uses a single prompt, some models above 200b parameters are quantised, closed-source model details are unavailable, and proxy failures caused some evaluation rows to be removed. The measured composite downstream score is not pretraining loss, and the paper does not fit or validate a scaling-law predictor.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing results were reported. The reasoning-enabled versus disabled comparisons in Figure 2 concern the effect of reasoning, not the scaling-law relations in the claim.

untested.parts: Whether downstream performance is predictable from a fitted law or extrapolates. No fit is made, no prediction is tested, and pretraining loss is never measured.
Not tested: no pretraining loss measured.
Not tested: no fits or extrapolation.
Not tested: no other modality or regime with a power-law fit.
Not tested: no fitting choices or exponents compared.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is figure-only, with no numbers, uncertainty or fit. The cross-family pooled comparison confounds compute with data and recipe. Large models (>200B) were quantised, and proxy failures removed some evaluation rows for closed models. The Related Works statements on Kaplan and Hoffmann are citations only.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude.
Whether fits from small runs predict substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study compares a composite travel-domain benchmark score with approximate training compute and model size; it does not test performance against pretraining loss or establish downstream predictability from a fitted law.

It does not compare fitting choices or exponents, compute-optimal splits, or loss curves. Its reported nonlinear downstream benchmark trend is not a test of the version's pretraining-loss fit-dependence claim.

rows.subject: 67 LLMs (aggregate benchmark results)
rows.operation_detail: Compared composite benchmark performance with approximate training compute (FLOPs ≈ 6NT).

conditions.value: TravelBench composite performance averaged over valid tasks

rows.measure: Composite scaled performance Pm versus training compute.
rows.note: The text describes a positive correlation, but says improvements diminish past approximately 0.5 ∗ 10^16 FLOPs and become slow and non-linear. Figure values are not transcribed in the text.
rows.check: The subject is not all 67 models. The limitations say closed-source models lack size and data details and were excluded from the FLOPs figure, so R1 covers only open models with known N and T. The plateau threshold '0.5*10^16 FLOPs' is implausibly small for 6NT of modern LLMs and is likely an axis-unit or typo issue; treat the threshold value as unreliable. Models from different families and data mixes are pooled, so compute is confounded with family. State partial is kept: there is a positive correlation, but gains are slow and non-linear past the threshold, and no predictive fit is given.

rows.subject: Qwen3 family models (aggregate across model sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Compared performance variation across model sizes on the benchmark tasks.
rows.measure: Benchmark performance and its spread across tasks as model size increases.
rows.note: The authors state that larger models are better on average, but performance consistency improvements are insignificant and task-level spread does not follow the same pattern. This is an aggregate family result; no plotted values are given in the text.
rows.check: The row merges two results. The first: 'larger models are on average better' within Qwen3, a same-data family, which is observed for the mean. The second: 'improvements in performance consistency are insignificant' and spread across tasks does not follow size. Partial is acceptable for the merged row, but the mean gain should ideally be a separate observed row. Exact sizes (8 hybrid models up to 235B) are omitted from size_stated.

relationships.condition: Open models' composite travel-benchmark score vs approximate training FLOPs; Qwen3 family mean score vs size
relationships.reason: The authors report a positive performance–compute correlation across tasks (R1), and larger Qwen3 models are better on average (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Performance correlated positively with approximate training compute across tasks, and larger Qwen3 models achieved higher average scores.

relationships.condition: Higher-compute models in a low-resource, domain-specific setting; per-task performance within Qwen3
relationships.reason: Gains become 'slow non-linear' past the stated compute threshold and models hit domain bottlenecks (R1). Task-level spread does not improve with size, so gains are task-dependent (R2). Evidence is figure-only, with no fit.
relationships.display_finding: Gains became slow and nonlinear at higher compute, while domain bottlenecks and persistent task-level variation prevented uniform improvement with size.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
